blocks.text: #3 Choice of the sensing platform, and why biology
June 5, 2026 | Assistant Professor Huang, Post-Baccalaureate Program in Medicine, National Tsing Hua University

Given the CSO's framing — selectivity and sensitivity are where the market is actually stuck — we evaluated why AeroSense's approach (insect olfactory receptors expressed in a mammalian cell line, read out via calcium fluorescence) is structurally different from a metal-oxide, polymer, or piezoelectric electronic nose, rather than just a biological curiosity layered on top of the same old approach.

A conventional electronic nose's sensing element is a fixed chemical material: it cannot be "reprogrammed" to a new target without physically replacing the sensor, and its selectivity is set by whatever cross-reactive chemistry that material happens to have. Our sensing element is a living, self-renewing receptor — the cell continuously synthesizes fresh copies of the Drosophila olfactory receptor (OR/Orco) and the GCaMP6 calcium reporter, so the sensing layer does not age or drift the way a static chemical film does, and the receptor itself can in principle be swapped for a different one (a different odorant receptor gene) to reprogram what the cartridge detects — directly addressing the CSO's "current sensors just aren't good enough" critique at the level of the sensing element itself, not the electronics around it.

This choice carries its own regulatory and biosafety considerations, which we address plainly rather than glossing over: the sensing cartridges use a genetically modified mammalian cell line (HEK293T expressing the olfactory receptor and calcium reporter), which requires standard biosafety-level handling and institutional biosafety oversight, and will eventually require university technology-transfer engagement given the receptor and neuromorphic-layer IP originates from institute research. No live insect material is used at any point — the receptor is heterologously expressed in a standard, well-characterized human cell line — which keeps biosafety handling considerably simpler at partner sites than a live-insect-based sensor would be.
#4 Investigating receptor candidates, and a direct hit from later analysis
September 10, 2026 | Founder Lin, Challenge Bio

Not every olfactory receptor is useful for our purposes, so receptor choice had to be evidence-driven rather than arbitrary. Our seven candidate receptors — Or10a, Or13a, Or47a, Or49b, Or71a, Or85b, and Or98a — were selected and sequenced based on Zboray et al. (2023, Scientific Reports), a heterologous-expression ligand-profiling study that itself was built to detect volatile plant and plant-pathogen biomarkers — meaning our starting receptor library was tuned toward fungal/plant VOCs, not bacterial ones.

This mattered directly when we later worked through the Challenge Bio interview's technical follow-up (see Box #6): mapping candidate pathogen-indicator VOCs against our existing seven-receptor library, we found that Or49b already has independent literature support for high sensitivity to indole — the classic volatile marker of E. coli/E. coli O157:H7 contamination — meaning this specific bacterial target could, in principle, be tested with a receptor we have already cloned, with no new receptor-discovery work required. We also found, and want to state honestly rather than overclaim, that a second apparent match — Or13a's well-characterized primary ligand, 1-octen-3-ol — is scientifically better known as a fungal volatile marker ("mushroom alcohol") than a bacteria-specific one, so it strengthens our original mold/food-safety receptor case rather than the newer bacterial-pathogen direction. Getting this distinction right, rather than quietly conflating the two, is exactly the kind of self-correction Human Practices is supposed to produce.
#5 Hardware and signal extraction

A sensitive receptor is only as useful as the electronics that can read a faint fluorescence signal out of real-world noise. This is the CSO's point, that sensitivity in the lab often collapses in the field, and it is why we treated the readout circuit as a design problem of its own.

Our first readout failed outside the lab. It used a blue LED and a camera. It worked on the bench, but once we left controlled conditions, ambient light and sensor noise swamped the faint cell signal. We replaced it with a lock-in design: the excitation light is modulated at a known frequency, and digital lock-in amplification (DLIA) reads only the signal at that frequency, rejecting room light and slow drift. We are candid about its limits. Excitation light that leaks onto the detector at the same frequency survives lock-in, so emission filtering, blank wells and per-well calibration are still needed.
Then we asked people with more hardware experience to check it. A circuit that only we had reviewed was the weakest link in the chain, so we took it to two sources of outside engineering advice.
September 21, 2026 | iST Group's engineering team

Over several rounds, iST engineers reviewed our sensing circuit and board design and helped us get from schematic to a manufactured prototype. They checked how the photodiode was connected, the design of the first amplification stage, the signal-conversion wiring and filtering, and the power and grounding arrangement. They also helped us reposition the light source and detector so that the weak signal path stays short, and, across successive revisions, settle the parts list, sourcing and timeline. The most useful lesson came from testing the finished board. The first amplification stage had too much gain, so its output sat at saturation whatever the light level. The engineers advised us to try feedback components of different values until the gain matched the photocurrent we actually produce, rather than trusting our calculated figure. We could not yet confirm the fix: the test firmware and a matching test setup were not ready, so only the main power supply was measured before the board reached us.
September 25, 2026 | A senior student with circuit-design experience

She came at the problem from the component side. She advised choosing the photodiode by its measured photocurrent, spectral response and current–voltage behavior, ideally with a device simulation, and confirming that the fluorescent protein's absorption and the light source's drive voltage actually match. For amplification she recommended a simple single-amplifier design with a suitable input range and a small feedback capacitor for stability and noise, and checking that the signal fits the converter's input range. She also stressed clean power, with proper smoothing at the regulator, and layout habits that cut noise: sensible trace routing, keeping the amplifier beside the detector, and large ground areas.

What changed. Three things. We now select the detector by its measured behavior instead of by what was convenient. Gain tuning, a signal measurement against known light levels, and then system integration are our next steps, in that order. And noise reduction, power stability and grounding moved from "later" to explicit goals of the next board revision. Where the hardware stands today: a first prototype board has been fabricated, but only its main power supply has been verified; light detection and signal conversion are untested until the firmware is ready.

Computation. A neuromorphic classification layer modeled on the fly mushroom body's PN–KC–MBON odor-coding circuit, with a direct, published research lineage through our own advisors' Science Advances 2025 paper, turns the raw multi-channel signal into a classification.
#6 Refining the beachhead and the target-selection framework
Our application focus has gone through two rounds of significant, evidence-driven revision — and we want the wiki to show both, not just the final answer.
Round one (mentor review, BP and pitch-deck feedback).
August 15, 2026 | Industry Mentors (Investors), From IP to IPO (FITI) Program

Our original framing covered six candidate crops (dragon fruit, passion fruit, strawberry, grape, citrus, banana) under a broad "facility agriculture pest detection" umbrella. Mentor review was blunt about the effect this had: "Right now it reads more like 'we have an electronic-nose technology that can do a lot of things,' but FITI needs to see 'a specific group of customers with a clear, expensive problem — and our odor detection directly reduces their loss, raises their price, or sets a new standard.'" This drove us to narrow to a single, economically quantifiable beachhead — banana disease detection in Taiwan's export supply chain — with mango and tea as explicit follow-on markets, and to reframe the whole narrative as a B2B Agricultural VOC Intelligence Platform rather than a general-purpose electronic nose.
Round two (Challenge Bio interview).
September 10, 2026 | Founder Lin, Challenge Bio
Introduction

AeroSense turns smell into actionable data — a biologically-inspired, AI-driven volatile organic compound (VOC) sensing platform built around a living olfactory receptor layer, custom lock-in optoelectronic hardware, and a neuromorphic classifier modeled on the fly brain. Human Practices(HP) guided every stage of this project: not as an add-on, but as the mechanism by which a technically impressive piece of synthetic biology became a product someone would actually buy, trust, and use correctly.

Through completed interviews spanning agricultural field sites, industry electronic-nose specialists, food-safety biotechnology professionals, and mentor review panels, plus a public survey probing food-spoilage habits and trust in automated screening tools, we built a working understanding of where our sensing platform's real value lies — and, just as importantly, where it does not.
Values

Our mission — let machines smell at a biological level, and turn odor into a measurable data dimension — is only worth pursuing if it is built responsibly. Three values have anchored every design decision:
（有圖示）

Early, not just accurate. A result that arrives after the batch has already spoiled or shipped is not useful, however accurate it is. We optimize for detecting change before it is visible — the entire premise of a VOC platform.

Honest about uncertainty. Our own stakeholders — from industry engineers to the general public in our survey — told us they distrust a black-box binary verdict more than an imperfect one they can see the confidence behind. We report a risk tier and a confidence signal, not a false promise of certainty.

Modularity over a single fixed claim. Our platform is a programmable receptor library, not a device hard-wired to one target. That flexibility is also a discipline: it forces us to prove, target by target, that a claim is scientifically defensible before we make it — rather than assuming our first application (mold detection) was automatically the right one.

#1 Problem
August 10, 2026 | Assistant Researcher Ya-Yun Chang, Plant Protection Laboratory, Taoyuan District Agricultural Research and Extension Station, Ministry of Agriculture

Every batch of produce, and every jar of dried food, starts to change before anyone can see it. Fungal disease in a banana shipment, or mold and toxin risk in stored coffee and grain, both release specific volatile organic compounds (VOCs) days to weeks before any visible symptom appears. By the time a packing-house inspector or a home cook sees the problem, the batch has often already been shipped, mixed with healthy stock, or eaten.

Today's detection options are split between two poor choices: visual/manual inspection (fast, but symptom-only — the infection has usually already spread by the time it's visible) and laboratory assays such as PCR, ELISA, or GC-MS (accurate, but slow, destructive, and impractical to run continuously across a full shipment). For Taiwan's banana export sector alone, we estimate potential fungal-disease-related loss at roughly NT$3.51 billion/year — about 33.6% of the sector's NT$10.445 billion annual output value. The same blind spot — a real signal hiding in plain smell, invisible until it's too late — motivated our earlier work on food-safety mold/mycotoxin screening for stored coffee, tea, and dried goods.

Both problem framings share the same underlying insight, one which our own public survey later reinforced from the consumer side: most respondents understood that visible mold is a problem, but only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk. Many people therefore judge by sight and smell, and have no way to know whether a specific portion is actually a problem. The tool that's missing isn't better education about mold; it's a way to know, cheaply and in minutes, whether this specific batch is actually a problem.

Checking the problem in the field. We took this question to the Plant Protection Lab of the Taoyuan District Agricultural Improvement Station. A researcher there confirmed the gap from the grower's side: there is currently no monitoring method beyond looking at the crop, so no data are collected. The researcher then asked us the questions a farmer would: first confirm that the device can collect data, and for which disease; what the device would look like in a field, how many sampling points a plot would need, and what the returned data would mean; and that buying or licensing an instrument depends on the crop and the target. The researcher also mentioned an earlier proposal to drive a remote-controlled vehicle through a tea field to collect electronic-nose data — possible in theory, but still far from practical on uneven ground. We took this as a reminder that "detects a smell" and "works in a field" are different claims.
#2 Key considerations for the sensor: what would actually help industry (Chief Science Officer interview)
September 11, 2026 | Professor Cheng, Enosim Bio-Tech

Before committing further engineering effort, we needed to know what a VOC sensor would have to do to be genuinely useful to people who already work with electronic-nose technology every day — not just what would make a compelling demo. We interviewed the Chief Science Officer (CSO) of an established domestic electronic-nose company Enosim Bio-Tech, whose own product line has already been evaluated against real deployment conditions.
The conversation reframed our engineering priorities around four properties, in this order of difficulty:

Selectivity — a sensor that responds strongly and specifically to the target gas, not broadly to A, B, C, and D at once. The CSO was direct about the state of the market: almost no commercially available electronic nose today has genuinely high selectivity.

Sensitivity — how low a concentration (down to ppm-level) the sensor can still detect, with a signal-to-noise ratio good enough to survive outside a quiet lab. This was flagged as the single most common failure mode: sensors that perform well on the bench become unusably noisy in a real field or warehouse environment.

Reliability and lifetime — how long a sensor can be used before its response degrades. Replacing a sensor daily, as some current products effectively require, is not a workable answer for continuous monitoring (e.g., air-quality deployments).

Reproducibility, including batch-to-batch consistency — does the same measurement, repeated, give the same answer; and do 100 units of the same sensor behave the same way as each other. This is a manufacturing-and-QA problem as much as a chemistry problem, and one the CSO said the industry still has not solved well.

The CSO's own framing of where the real difficulty lies was the most consequential single insight from this conversation: "Right now, sensors just aren't good enough — the hardware and the algorithms are the easy part." In other words, the bottleneck the industry actually faces is the sensing element itself (selectivity, sensitivity, stability, reproducibility) — not the downstream electronics or signal processing. This is a direct, external validation of AeroSense's core technical bet: that a living, self-renewing biological olfactory receptor — evolved over millions of years for exactly this kind of selective, sensitive chemical discrimination — is a more defensible place to compete than trying to out-engineer conventional metal-oxide or polymer sensor materials on selectivity alone.

We treat this interview as belonging to the same evidence category as our technical-loop interviews: it does not tell us what to sell, but it does tell us the bar our sensing layer has to clear to be worth selling at all — and it directly shaped how we now describe our differentiation (see Box #4 and #6).

Just as we had converged on a single beachhead, a separate conversation with biotechnology industry professionals challenged the premise underneath our original food-safety framing, not the agricultural one: "Start from the technology, not the application" — establish what AeroSense can actually distinguish (detectable VOCs, specificity, sensitivity, response time, interference tolerance) before assuming any one market is the right one. Just as importantly: "mold VOCs do not necessarily represent food safety" — food processing can kill viable fungi or change their odor profile while a toxin such as aflatoxin remains, so a mold-VOC signal and an actual safety verdict are not the same claim, and we should not let our own marketing imply otherwise.

This produced a new, explicit target-selection framework — Detectability × Consequence × Unmet Need × Willingness to Pay — which we are now applying systematically rather than defaulting back to "mold detection" out of habit (including the E. coli/indole/Or49b finding in Box #4).
Round three (analytical-instrumentation industry interview).
September 17, 2026 | SCIEX Field Service Engineer Lin (LC and GC–MS Maintenance)

We interviewed a professional with hands-on GC-MS/LC-MS testing-service experience Engineer to answer a question the first two rounds had left open: should AeroSense compete with laboratory instruments on analytical accuracy, or solve a different problem entirely? Their answer showed that our original assumption — that AeroSense would be "a cheaper alternative to conventional analytical instruments" — did not hold on the numbers: a GC-MS/LC-MS system's amortized cost (roughly NT$5–10 million over a ~15-year service life, plus NT$200,000–300,000/year maintenance, per the interviewee) is not the barrier we assumed; the real barriers are trained personnel and lab infrastructure, which is why the industry itself is already moving toward smaller and mobile testing units. We therefore repositioned our value proposition around three words the interviewee's account of the market supported: Fast · On-site · Low operator dependence — a rapid on-site screening layer that flags suspicious samples for laboratory confirmation, not a replacement for the lab.

Two further findings reshaped our thinking. First, individual farmers may have low willingness to pay and may resist having their own product flagged as a problem, which shifts our realistic B2B buyer toward farmers' associations, agricultural agencies, cooperatives, and certification bodies. Second, the interview surfaced a candidate application we had not evaluated — authenticity and origin verification (e.g., honey origin, tea authenticity) — as a third candidate alongside disease/ripeness detection and pathogen-VOC food-safety screening, though with its own validation challenge, since false positives and blended samples are harder to resolve than a straightforward risk flag. The interviewee also named two segments we had not considered, the semiconductor industry and humanitarian/logistics shipping; we record them as leads from a single conversation, not validated opportunities. All figures here are the interviewee's own and we have not independently verified them.
Round four (field pathology interview).
September 25, 2026 | Min-Hsiung Weng, Retired Researcher, Taiwan Banana Research Institute

To test where odor-based screening would help most on a banana farm, we interviewed a pest-and-disease specialist at the Taiwan Banana Research Institute in Pingtung and went through his institute's growth-stage guide to banana pests and diseases. Two findings stood out. First, the strongest odors come from below ground and basal tissue, not from the fruit: corm and pseudostem weevils, bacterial soft rot, crown rot, and Fusarium wilt (Panama disease), which smells strongest in the corm's vascular tissue. Fruit-side problems such as scale insects, finger-tip rot, and cigar-end rot are not strongly scented, and sooty mold smells faint. Second, the odor of Fusarium wilt is most obvious late, when the plant is already rotting and visibly blackened; he told us a faint signal is present earlier, though usually only noticeable in the middle to late stage, and that detecting it is largely a matter of sensor sensitivity. He also cautioned that a heavy pseudostem smell often just reflects a dirty orchard, so any odor reading has to be interpreted against field hygiene, and he named rot detection as a problem farmers and field workers need solved.

The interview also touched on who would use a tool like ours. He indicated that an institute like his is more willing to pay than individual farmers, which matches what the instrumentation interview told us. His institute already covers rot testing and pest-and-disease control close to growers, so it could be an entry point that reaches farmers who cannot buy a tool themselves; we are considering its Pingtung site as a pilot. He also asked the question we cannot yet answer: can the method really measure accurately, and are there particular diseases or sites where it works best? This is an expert's qualitative judgment, not a measurement, so we treat it as a hypothesis to test — how many days earlier the faint signal appears, and whether it can be separated from background orchard odor. It also pushes us to weigh field-level rot detection alongside our original post-harvest focus.
#7.1 Business plan and scaling
March 2026 | NTHU Garage
July–September 2026 | FITI (From IP to IPO) Program

We engaged directly with startup-support programs and mentor panels to pressure-test our commercialization plan rather than developing it in isolation. Selection into FITI (From IP to IPO), Taiwan's national innovation and entrepreneurship incentive program, and the 18th cohort of NTHU Garage connected us to structured, written mentor review at two stages: an 11-point review of our full business plan, and a separate slide-level review of our pitch deck. Both reviews converged on the same underlying instruction — lead with a specific customer's expensive problem, not with the technology — but each forced a different layer of revision: the BP review drove the beachhead narrowing and a full TAM/SAM/SOM rebuild (from a benchmark against the global electronic-nose instrument market to a bottom-up agricultural-VOC estimate connected to actual banana-sector loss figures); the pitch-deck review drove the competitive-analysis redesign (comparing detectable-VOC range, detection limit, and fingerprinting ability rather than analysis cycle time, an axis where we are not competitive) and a shift from a name-and-photo team slide to a capability matrix. The full stage-by-stage record is in our FITI Iteration Report.

Our financial model reflects this same discipline: modeled, not promised, figures — a Year 1 operating expense of roughly NT$3.08 million against a NT$3 million seed round in progress, with device and cartridge pricing (device ~NT$120,000, cartridge subscription ~NT$4,000/month) drawn from the same workbook rather than invented for a slide.

#7.2 Protecting what we built: a patent attorney consultation
October 14, 2026 | Patent Attorney Hsu

We consulted a patent attorney whose main expertise is in pharmaceuticals and microbiology. She asked us for the related paper, the design process of our device with the reasoning behind each choice, and a clear statement of which technical step is the real innovation. She explained the three tests a patent must pass — novelty, an inventive step that others would not easily anticipate, and industrial applicability — and advised us to run a prior-art search before designing any strengthening experiments, since a disclosure on a website or in a paper counts as prior art. She also pointed out that a new use of a technology that others have not described can itself be patentable, and that results not yet made public are the strongest position for novelty.

She explained that the right route differs by what we protect: engineered protein variants fit an invention patent, which gets a full examination with a prior-art search and lasts 20 years, while a complete device or system may suit a utility model, which is examined for form only and lasts 10 years. From a start-up's point of view, he said, a utility model for the whole system may be the better fit. Whether to patent something or keep it as a trade secret is our decision, not his. She was not sure how infringement consequences differ between the two types, since he has not handled such cases, so we treat that as unanswered.

Her most consequential advice was about timing. Our own disclosures can later count as prior art; Taiwan allows a one-year grace period for the applicant's own disclosures, but China and Europe are stricter, so she advised filing first and publishing afterwards. The grace period protects only against our own disclosure, not against someone else who sees our work and files first. A provisional filing in the United States can secure an early filing date. When a university is a development partner, the university is usually the applicant, with students and advisors as inventors, so we plan to begin with the university's route and to settle our target countries before publishing technical detail.
#8 Impact
July 2026 | Public Survey

Positive impacts. By making early, non-destructive VOC screening cheap enough to run continuously rather than by sample, AeroSense aims to reduce both food loss (produce discarded or shipped unnecessarily late) and food waste driven by over-caution (our public survey found that only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk, so people throw out what may be fine or keep what is not — a screening tool that can say "this specific batch is fine" reduces needless waste as much as one that catches real risk reduces unsafe consumption). A growing, receptor-agnostic VOC platform also lowers the barrier for smaller exporters and cooperatives to access screening capability currently limited to buyers who can afford lab-grade testing.

Risks to manage. An automated risk score that is trusted too much invites exactly the failure mode our own stakeholders warned us about from two directions at once: our public survey found that respondents ranked avoiding a missed real risk (a false negative) among their top needs from a screening tool, and the Challenge Bio interview independently warned that a mold-VOC signal is not the same claim as a food-safety verdict. Both point to the same design discipline: report a risk tier with an honest confidence signal and a recommendation to send high-risk samples for confirmatory lab testing — never a silent, false "safe" — and say plainly, in our own materials, what the tool does not certify. We plan a lightweight, mentor-supported data-governance check-in as the platform moves from single-partner pilots to multi-partner deployment, extending the same "close the loop, don't just collect feedback" discipline documented throughout this page to how we handle an increasingly large, cross-partner VOC dataset.
#9 Handing the work on: from a science camp to a teacher toolkit
October 12, 2026 | Shan-chi Elementary School
Most of this page asks what outsiders told us about our project. The last loop we closed ran the other way: we took our project to a school, and the school told us what it needed from us.

What we assumed. After the survey and the games, we ran a half-day science camp at Shan-chi Elementary School in Xinfeng Township, Hsinchu County, on , for more than thirty pupils in grades 5 (the full account is on our Education page). We counted the camp itself as the finished product: a day in which children learned how a nose, an electronic nose and our sensor relate, played our game and drew what they imagined.

What we heard. We met the school's principal on the camp day. He told us he liked the way we teach, and he asked for a way to keep using it, since a team of university students cannot visit every year.

What it changed. His request moved the unit of impact from the visit to the lesson. If a school wants something it can keep using, a camp is the wrong thing to leave behind. We packaged the camp into a Teacher Toolkit: a 40-minute lesson with slides, a whole-class version of our game in which each team answers by holding up one, two or three fingers, a worksheet, and instructions for using our online Learning Lab, so that a teacher who has never met us can run the same session. The school welcomed the approach, and the toolkit is free for any teacher to download. The same conversation gave us the design rule that opens our Education Guide for other teams: write the plan so that someone who has never met you can run it.
Events

Throughout the duration of our iGEM project, we sought out events where we could speak with people already working in synthetic biology, biotechnology, agri-tech, and startup commercialization — not to collect endorsements, but to stress-test our assumptions against people who had no reason to be polite about them. Some of these encounters changed a specific number on a slide; others changed how we described the entire project. All of them are documented here with what we actually heard, not a polished summary of it — including the places where the feedback was blunt.

NTHU Garage Cohort (March 2026)
Our entry point into structured commercialization support was selection into the 18th cohort of NTHU Garage+, the university's entrepreneurship incubation program. This became our home base for the rest of the season: regular access to mentor office hours, a structured go-to-market and fundraising curriculum. NTHU Garage is where our very first business-plan draft took shape, before any of the external review rounds that reshaped it.

Collaboration with the S.Y.Dao Cancer Prevention Foundation (May 2026)
We reached out to the S.Y.Dao Cancer Prevention Foundation after learning that olfactory-based sensing had shown promise for early cancer detection — close enough to our own platform that we approached them on our own initiative rather than waiting for a polished pitch. Through the discussion, we brought our Food & Nutrition-track VOC findings together with our platform's potential medical application, rather than presenting the two as separate stories. The foundation responded positively to both the technology and its application potential.

SynBioBeta 2026 — NextGen Bioleader/Poster Session (May 2026)
We presented AeroSense's platform at SynBioBeta 2026, an international synthetic-biology industry conference, via a poster session aimed at an industry rather than academic audience. This was our first exposure to how people entirely outside our own university network — investors, industry scientists, and other synbio startups — reacted to the platform on first contact, without the context our own team takes for granted.

FITI — From IP to IPO / Future Innovation and Technology Initiative (July–September 2026)
Being selected into FITI, Taiwan's national innovation and entrepreneurship program, gave us structured mentorship support from both the Hsinchu Science Park and Central Taiwan Science Park bureaus — exactly the research-to-startup bridge a student team built out of a neuroscience lab most needed to move from a working platform toward something investable. 
Across a three-month review process, this connected us to written reviewer feedback, a mentor panel, and a separate pitch-deck review that together reshaped our business plan and go-to-market narrative; the specific feedback and the changes it drove are documented in full on our Entrepreneurship page.

Guest Sharing Session — China Medical University (September 2026) 
We were invited to share AeroSense in a neuroscience course at China Medical University — home institution of our academic advisor, Prof. Ching-Che Charng — introducing students to synthetic biology, the iGEM competition, and how we combined biology and engineering to build a working sensing platform. Presenting to an audience trained in neuroscience rather than synbio pushed us to explain our platform's biological logic more plainly than we do among our own team, and the discussion that followed was itself a useful test of how clearly we could tell our own story.

iGEM Mini Jamboree — organized by iGEM TAU, Tel-Aviv University (October 2026)
We took part in the iGEM Teams Meetup, an inter-team gathering organized by Tel Aviv University's iGEM team (iGEM TAU). The session connected us with teams from across the Americas, Europe, and Asia, and hearing how differently each team framed its own project was itself a useful check on our own assumptions. We're especially looking forward to meeting many of these teams in person at the November gathering.

Conclusion

Our Integrated Human Practices journey turned AeroSense from a promising piece of synthetic biology into a platform shaped by the people who'd actually use it — electronic-nose engineers, food-safety professionals, farmers, mentors, and the public we surveyed.

Their feedback pointed to the same gap from every angle: existing sensors aren't selective enough, and the real barrier to on-site testing isn't price but personnel and infrastructure. AeroSense answers this with a living, redirectable receptor and a Fast · On-site · Low-operator-dependence design — kept affordable enough for cooperatives and exporters alike, not just labs.
